results.title: Broadcom (AVGO) Pairs AI Chip Boom With A Software Security Push
results.author: Maham Fatima
results.content:
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) has drawn significant market attention in 2026 for its custom AI chips. But the company's August 6 announcement of new VMware vDefend and Avi Load Balancer capabilities is a reminder that its infrastructure software business, the one built to throw off steady, high-margin cash, is still evolving too. With the stock sitting roughly 20% below the all-time high it set at the end of May, investors are left weighing a fast-growing chip story against a market that has already pulled back once this year.
Bull Case: A Business Firing On Two Engines
The custom chip pipeline remains the headline growth driver. Chief Executive Hock Tan has told investors Broadcom's AI semiconductor business will top $100 billion in revenue in 2027, a jump from the $10.8 billion it generated in the second quarter alone, up 143% year over year. Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) is currently the primary buyer of those chips. Still, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and other major clients are expected to place larger orders once 2027 arrives, and Broadcom has already guided for its AI chip business to grow more than 200% in the current quarter. Total company revenue rose 48% year over year to $22.2 billion in the second quarter, adjusted earnings per share climbed 54% to $2.44, and free cash flow reached $10.3 billion, up 60%.
The August 6 vDefend and Avi Load Balancer update shows the software side isn't standing still either. The new releases, vDefend SSP 5.2, vDefend 9.1.1, Avi Load Balancer 32.1.4, and the vACT 3.0 migration tool, add native API protection, on-premises malware sandboxing, and full air-gapped support, while substantially boosting performance. Distributed Firewall throughput can now reach up to 75Gbps per 100G NIC server, a 241% increase, scaling to 75Tbps across a VMware Cloud Foundation instance, and Avi Load Balancer throughput per controller can climb to 12.25Tbps. A new two-node deployment model also cuts the hardware needed to run vDefend by as much as 33%. Broadcom is pitching this as a response to AI-fueled cyberattacks, giving enterprises a reason to expand their VMware footprint even as chip demand grabs the spotlight.
Bear Case: Concentration And A Cautious Market
The flip side of Broadcom's chip success is how few customers it depends on. Alphabet and Meta account for the bulk of custom silicon demand today, and while both have signed long-term agreements, Meta's running through 2029 and Alphabet's through 2031, any disruption to those relationships would ripple through the stock quickly. That risk helps explain why shares fell sharply after Broadcom's last earnings report despite results and guidance that pointed to accelerating AI chip sales. Valuation debates hinge heavily on which year of earnings investors use and how much multiple compression they expect once growth normalizes, with estimates for where the stock could trade in coming years varying by billions of dollars depending on small changes in assumptions.
results.summary:
Broadcom is balancing rapid growth in its custom AI semiconductor business with significant infrastructure software updates, even as investors weigh high customer concentration against strong financial performance.

### Key Points
- Broadcom projects its AI semiconductor revenue will exceed $100 billion by 2027, driven by major clients including Alphabet and Meta Platforms.
- Second-quarter revenue reached $22.2 billion, a 48% year-over-year increase, with adjusted earnings per share rising 54% to $2.44.
- The company released new VMware vDefend and Avi Load Balancer capabilities, featuring enhanced API protection and performance improvements of up to 241%.
- New software updates include a two-node deployment model designed to reduce hardware requirements for vDefend by 33%.
- Long-term supply agreements with Alphabet and Meta extend through 2029 and 2031, though heavy reliance on these two firms remains a primary investor concern.

### Why it Matters
Broadcom’s dual-engine strategy aims to sustain high-margin cash flow through software while capturing massive growth in the AI hardware market. The company's ability to mitigate risks associated with customer concentration will be critical for maintaining its valuation as market expectations for AI-driven growth continue to evolve.

results.title: 7 Best Tech Gadgets of August 2026
results.author: Srishti Mitra
results.content:
August arrives with a lineup that feels genuinely considered. Not every gadget this month is chasing a headline spec or fighting for shelf space. Some of the most interesting things landing right now are smaller, quieter, and more honest about what they actually do — a folding mouse that disappears into a shirt pocket, a bedside unit that replaces three devices at once, and a dual-screen E Ink tablet that finally treats reading and writing as a single workflow rather than two separate tasks competing for the same screen.
There’s also something larger worth paying attention to. Samsung is officially pulling back the curtain on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 this month, and what’s shaping up as a tiered foldable lineup could redefine the category’s identity. Meanwhile, Google has quietly slipped a new smart speaker onto store shelves for the first time in six years. August, as it turns out, rewards patience — and knowing exactly where to look.
1. piBrick Pocket-CM5
The piBrick Pocket-CM5 is one of those projects that reads better the longer you spend with the spec sheet. Built by Ahmad Amarullah on a custom PCB designed around the Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, this open-source handheld costs around $172 in parts and arrives at smartphone proportions — 80 × 145 × 19.6mm. The 3.92-inch AMOLED display runs at 1080 × 1240 and 90Hz with Asahi tempered glass over the top, which is the kind of detail that separates a deliberate design from a prototype that merely happens to work. Full-size and micro-HDMI outputs mean the same pocket device can drive an external display when a larger workspace makes more sense.
The BBQ20 keyboard with its integrated BlackBerry-derived trackpad gives the piBrick a tactile depth that touchscreen-only handhelds cannot match, and side rotary encoders plus five programmable buttons extend the input options further still. A 5,000mAh LiPo keeps everything running, NVMe SSD support in 2230 or 2242 formats handles storage, and USB 3.0 with Type-A and Type-C covers connectivity. The most quietly useful feature is USB-HID mode — plug the piBrick into any external machine and its keyboard and trackpad instantly become a functional input device, independent of the Pi entirely. For a sysadmin who shows up at a server rack without a spare keyboard, that framing changes the device from hobbyist novelty to legitimate daily carry tool.
What we like:
- USB-HID mode turns the whole device into a USB keyboard for any external computer
- 90Hz AMOLED at this price point and form factor is a genuinely rare combination
What we dislike:
- Requires hands-on sourcing, PCB manufacturing, and 3D-printed shell assembly
- The compact BBQ20 keyboard layout carries a real learning curve for extended typing sessions
2. OrigamiSwift Folding Mouse
The OrigamiSwift is a Bluetooth mouse that folds flat to 0.18 inches — thinner than most notepads — and springs back into a full-size ergonomic form in under half a second. Designed by Horace Lam and built around the geometry of traditional origami folding, it weighs just 40 grams and connects over Bluetooth 5.2, with a 4,000 CPI HD infrared sensor tracking at up to 30 inches per second. For digital nomads and frequent travelers, the appeal is immediate: full-size mousing comfort that compresses to the front pocket of a bag without any structural compromise.
Soft-click buttons and a smooth, consistent glide make it discreet in quiet environments, and the triangular origami structure that enables the folding mechanism also gives the frame enough rigidity to absorb daily use without flex. Battery life is a genuine standout — one USB-C charge lasts up to three months, which removes the disposable battery cycle from the equation entirely. At $85, it sits in a price range where compromises tend to accumulate, and the sensor performance, weight, and build quality keep most of them from appearing. It works across Mac, iPad, Windows, and Android without additional drivers, which keeps the setup frictionless wherever you end up working.
What we like:
- Three-month battery life on a single USB-C charge is genuinely exceptional for a wireless mouse
- 40 grams means you stop noticing it’s in your bag until the moment you actually need it
What we dislike:
- 4,000 CPI ceiling may not satisfy users working on high-resolution or multi-monitor setups
- Stock is currently very limited, with only a few units available in the shop
3. Divoom FlowToo
The Divoom FlowToo costs $99.99 and replaces three things that have been quietly cluttering nightstands for years — a Bluetooth speaker, a white noise machine, and an alarm clock. It runs through a 10W amplifier with a 45mm full-range driver, which is enough to fill a bedroom at a respectable volume without the sound becoming harsh at the high end. More than 90 built-in sounds cover the categories people actually reach for at night and during focus sessions, from rain and ocean ambience to forest and calming tones, and the Divoom app handles everything from alarm scheduling to sound selection directly from your phone.
The 2.26-inch smart display is the part that makes the FlowToo feel like something designed with some care rather than assembled from a parts list. It cycles between multiple clock faces, music visualizers that react to whatever’s playing, sleep scene animations, and mood lighting depending on the mode and the time of day. The wake-up sequence replaces a jarring alarm tone with natural sounds that build in volume while the display gradually brightens — a small change that makes a real difference to how the first few minutes of a morning feel. Available in White and Black, the form is clean, rounded, and scaled well enough to sit beside most beds without dominating the surface.
What we like:
- A 10W full-range driver makes this a real speaker, not just an alarm clock with Bluetooth bolted on
- The gradual light-and-sound wake sequence is a meaningfully better way to start the morning
What we dislike:
- Dedicated white noise machines and standalone speakers will each outperform the FlowToo in their respective categories
- Full feature access requires the Divoom app, which adds dependency to a device built around simplicity
4. Portable CD Cover Player
The Portable CD Cover Player brings album artwork back to the physical center of the listening experience at a time when streaming has reduced most music libraries to a scrollable grid of thumbnails no larger than a postage stamp. The form factor is slim and designed to echo the proportions of a CD sleeve — built for the kind of listening that happens away from a desk, on a commute, in a hotel room, or anywhere else a record player cannot reasonably follow you without significant planning.
There is something the CD format offers that streaming still hasn’t managed to replicate — intentionality. You chose this album. You put it in. You listened front to back, the way it was meant to be heard. The Portable CD Cover Player leans into that ritual rather than treating it as an inconvenience to be engineered away. At a moment when cassette players and vinyl decks have staged a credible commercial comeback, there is a real and growing audience for physical music hardware that does not apologize for existing in 2026. For anyone rebuilding a CD collection or looking for a reason to use the one they never threw out, this is the device for it.
What we like:
- Restores album artwork as a physical, tactile part of the listening experience rather than a compressed thumbnail
- The intentionality of the CD format is something streaming genuinely cannot replicate
What we dislike:
- The price requires an existing or rebuilt CD collection to justify the investment
- Stock is tight, with only a few units currently available through the Yanko Design shop
5. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
Samsung confirmed the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Unpacked event for July 22 in London, and what’s taking shape is arguably the most architecturally ambitious foldable lineup the company has attempted. Three models appear to be in play — the standard Fold 8 at 4.1mm unfolded, the wide-format Fold 8 Wide at a remarkable 3.9mm, and the Fold 8 Ultra, which is where the S Pen is making its return after being stripped from the Fold 7 to achieve that device’s headline thinness. Reports point to a titanium-plus-carbon-fiber construction for the Ultra, a material combination that works more naturally with the digitizer layer the stylus requires than the pure titanium backplate the Fold 7 used.
The Ultra is the model worth watching most closely. A 5,000mAh battery — the largest in the Fold line since the third generation — marks the first meaningful capacity upgrade the series has seen in years, and the S Pen’s return shifts the Fold 8 Ultra from a premium hardware story into something with actual software depth for power users. Samsung is also reportedly developing a digitizer-free stylus solution for future generations, which would eventually decouple S Pen functionality from physical bulk entirely. If the Ultra ships as the leaks describe, it becomes the first Z Fold that stops treating its own productivity features as a problem to be engineered around, and starts treating them as the reason the device exists.
What we like:
- S Pen returns on the Ultra alongside the line’s largest battery to date
- A tiered lineup lets buyers choose between thinness-first or capability-first without compromise
What we dislike:
- Splitting S Pen support exclusively to the Ultra positions it as a premium within an already premium product line
- Three distinct SKUs risk diluting the design identity that made the Fold recognizable in the first place
6. Google Home Speaker
The Google Home Speaker is the company’s first new standalone smart speaker since the Nest Audio launched in September 2020. Nearly six years is a long time to leave a product category untouched in consumer electronics — Apple refreshed AirPods three times in that window, Sonos shipped new hardware, redesigned its app, and broke it, and still found time to come back. Google’s return is framed almost entirely around Gemini, now built directly into the speaker and positioned as the primary reason to put it on your kitchen counter rather than any particular advancement in audio engineering.
The hardware reads clean — small, rounded, and available in the kind of understated colors Google’s design teams have always been good at selecting. It features 360-degree audio, faster processing for more fluid conversational responses, and a new light ring that signals when Gemini is listening, thinking, or responding. Whether this launch represents a genuine recommitment to the smart home category or simply Google finding Gemini another product surface to occupy is a fair question to ask. The speaker is back on the counter after six years. Whether the company chooses to stay in the room this time is the harder and more important question.
What we like:
- Gemini integration makes this the most conversationally capable Google speaker the company has ever shipped
- Six years of hardware and processing advancement mean the gap over the Nest Audio should be substantial
What we dislike:
- Google’s well-documented history of deprioritizing smart home hardware makes long-term software support a legitimate concern
- The launch narrative frames the speaker as AI infrastructure first, and as a designed product second
7. Inkleaf Foldable Dual-Screen E Ink Notebook
The Inkleaf is a foldable dual-screen E Ink tablet with two 10.3-inch Carta panels that open side by side — one for reading, one for writing, simultaneously. That single feature solves a problem researchers, students, and writers have been navigating awkwardly for years, usually by propping a tablet next to a paper notebook or toggling between apps and losing their place each time. Designed by Kameron Yu, it closes to 8.4mm and 480 grams, thinner than a standard paperback, and each open panel measures 4.2mm — slimmer than the reMarkable 2 at 4.7mm, the Kindle Scribe at 5.4mm, and the Boox Note Air4 C at 5.8mm. None of those fold.
The cast aluminum body and precision-machined hinge barrel lay perfectly flat at 180 degrees when open, tactile page-turn buttons sit exactly where your thumb expects them, and the pressure-sensitive stylus ships in the box with no subscription fee attached. Android handles the OS with support for PDFs, EPUBs, MOBI, and TXT files, and an AI-powered handwriting search can surface any phrase across every notebook you’ve filled. First units are expected to reach founders in August 2026. At around $450, it is a serious financial commitment, but one the form factor and the problem it actually solves manage to earn.
What we like:
- Dual-screen setup genuinely resolves the read-and-write-simultaneously problem that every comparable single-screen device ignores
- 4.2mm per panel open is thinner than any single-screen E Ink device currently on the market
What we dislike:
- The price point requires a real commitment to the E Ink workflow to justify
- Android on an E Ink display still carries limitations in app responsiveness and screen refresh speed
August Belongs to the Gadgets That Get Out of the Way
August’s lineup doesn’t follow a single theme, which is part of what makes it worth paying attention to. The piBrick and the Inkleaf both treat computing as something that should fit your actual workflow rather than just your desk. The OrigamiSwift and the FlowToo make the case that the best everyday tech is the kind that removes something from your bag or your nightstand rather than quietly adding to it. The Portable CD Cover Player is a reminder that intentional listening never actually went away — it just needed hardware worth using again.
The bigger stories — Samsung’s Fold 8 and Google’s long-overdue speaker — tell you something meaningful about where two of the industry’s largest companies have landed on the question of what smart hardware is actually for. One is restoring capability it arguably should never have removed. The other is making up for six years of silence with an AI pitch and hoping nobody checks the calendar. Both are worth watching this month, for very different reasons.
results.summary:
August brings a diverse wave of consumer technology, ranging from niche open-source handhelds and foldable E Ink tablets to major hardware updates from industry giants like Samsung and Google.

### Key Points
- The piBrick Pocket-CM5 is an open-source, Raspberry Pi-based handheld featuring a 3.92-inch AMOLED display and a unique USB-HID mode for external device control.
- Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy Z Fold 8 lineup introduces a tiered strategy, including an Ultra model that restores S Pen support and features a 5,000mAh battery.
- The Inkleaf foldable tablet utilizes dual 10.3-inch E Ink screens to allow simultaneous reading and writing, measuring just 4.2mm per panel when open.
- Google has released its first standalone smart speaker in six years, focusing on Gemini AI integration and 360-degree audio capabilities.
- The OrigamiSwift Bluetooth mouse offers a collapsible, origami-inspired design that folds to 0.18 inches thick with a three-month battery life.
- The Divoom FlowToo consolidates a Bluetooth speaker, white noise machine, and alarm clock into a single bedside unit with a customizable smart display.

### Why it Matters
These product launches highlight a shift toward hardware that prioritizes specific user workflows and physical minimalism over generic feature sets. By focusing on intentional design and specialized utility, these devices challenge the industry to move beyond iterative updates and address the actual needs of modern digital environments.

results.title: Incentives Are for Losers
results.author: Adam Mastroianni
results.content:
Incentives are for losers
OR: you must look at this fish and go insane
We can all agree: the incentives are bad. Everywhere you look, people are being rewarded for doing the wrong thing. This has become the go-to diagnosis for every problem, from climate change to political polarization to scientific malfeasance—“sorry pal, you’ve got a bad case of the incentives.”
I don’t disagree with this analysis, exactly. Who could? It’s basically tautological. “People do bad things because they are encouraged and rewarded for doing bad things.” Well, why else would you do them?
My real gripe with this line of thinking is it implies that incentives should be obeyed, that it is normal or even noble to do so, and that is perhaps impossible to do otherwise. How could you be expected to break a rule, forego a promotion, or give up decimal of your grade point average, for the sake of—what? Doing the right thing?
There’s a point here that should go without saying, but instead it has simply gone unsaid. Which is: incentives are for losers. Doing something simply because an arbitrary reward system will give you a lil treat—that’s for pigeons, not people. If you build your life around satisfying incentives, then you’re a dummy and a schmuck.1
COME HELMET OR HIGH WATER
When I played Little League baseball for a few disastrous years, my least favorite part was going up to bat, because you had to wear one of these ratty old batting helmets supplied by the local rec department. None of them fit right, and they all smelled like a hundred sweaty 10-year-olds had worn them before you, because a hundred sweaty 10-year-olds had worn them before you. And so every at-bat carried not only the risk of striking out, but also the risk of contracting head lice.2
A few kids, the serious ones, brought their own helmets—custom fitted, tastefully decorated with decals, and presumably containing zero lice. These kids ran the bases like little princes. Any errant pitches bounced harmlessly off their heads, leaving their perfect skulls un-dented. The outfielders would perk up whenever a kid with a bespoke helmet stepped up to the plate, all of them thinking to themselves, this kid might actually hit the ball.
I say all this because incentives are like batting helmets: if you don’t bring your own, you’ll have to use the crappy ones that are provided for you.
A critical part of human development—in fact, the most human part of human development—is to acquire a purpose. That means refining your sense of right and wrong and figuring out how you, personally, can increase the right and decrease the wrong. Once your neural tube has ballooned into a brain, once you can poop without issue, conjugate irregular verbs, and feed yourself solid foods, you ought to ask yourself, “Why am I doing these things?” What’s it all for? How can I make myself useful?
It’s fine if you’re still working on your answers to those questions. It’s fine—and good!—if you have multiple answers, or if your answers change over time. But it’s not fine to pass on the questions entirely. We owe these answer to each other, and we owe them to ourselves, because a sense of purpose is both prosocial and protective. If you have a void where your moral convictions should be, then that cavity of your personality will get filled up with tumorous desires—for money, power, fame, status. This is the kind of person who “responds to incentives”.
It took me a long time to understand this. In my early 20s, when I was at the bottom of every ladder that I aspired to ascend, I assumed the people at the top of those ladders must be pretty great. How wise these incentive-maxxers must be, how cool and smart, to have the things that everybody else wants!
But over the years, as I had the opportunity to meet some of these captains of industry, these Grand Pooh-Bahs and Distinguished Scholars, I’ve realized how wrong I was. They only seemed enviable because I was looking at them from a distance, so all I could see was what they had. Up close, when you can see what they are, it becomes clear that only a few of these ladder-toppers are indeed wise and cool. More often, they’re sniveling little twerps. They’re spiritually chinless. They have no convictions, no passions, no purpose other than ladder-climbing. It’s sad to watch them, these people who have everything except the one thing that actually matters.
Often, these are the people who are most insistent that the incentives ought to be obeyed. They are quick to swear that good grades, cash, prestige, etc. are inherently valuable, or that they are useful proxies for value. The incentive-obsessives feel this way because they have to. Like the government of a failing nation, they must swear that their currency is real, and they must lash out at anyone attempting to participate in an alternative economy, lest the whole fraud come crashing down upon itself.
HELP ME, SKY DADDY, YOU’RE MY ONLY HOPE
Without any formal instruction, approximately 100% of humans will learn to speak, and approximately 0% of humans will learn to read. Talking comes easy and early, enabled by ancient mental structures that hoover up words and extract the meaning behind them. These are the original LLMs, and still the best in the known universe. Reading, on the other hand, comes late and laboriously, piggybacking on bits of brain that were never meant to decode squiggles on paper, let alone comprehend Finnegans Wake.
So when thinking about any human ability, it’s useful to ask: is this more like speaking, or is it more like reading? Is this an ancient capability that we get for free just by living long enough, or is this a modern skill that you can’t get without working for it?
Developing a value system seems to be a lot more like reading, because research suggests that many people don’t make it very far.
In the early 2000s, the sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton asked hundreds of American teenagers about their religious beliefs. What they got in return was a bunch of gobbledygook. Regardless of their supposed faith, few of these teens could say anything specific about the divine. Most of them believed that God is like, this cool dude who floats in the sky and wants everybody to be happy and to get along, and if you ask him nicely he might help you achieve your goals, but otherwise he’s mostly busy floating. Fortunately, this celestial butler is not super specific about what you should and shouldn’t do, and he doesn’t really speak unless spoken to.3
Smith and Denton came up with a name for this thin soup of theology: moralistic therapeutic deism. They only studied teenagers, but they suspect that many people remain moralistic therapeutic deists for their whole lives—after all, the teens probably picked up this loose handful of beliefs from their parents. People will claim on surveys that they belong to a certain religion, or they’ll get riled up about specific bits of dogma. But if you dig into their beliefs at all, you’ll soon hit a gooey core of underbaked religious mishmash.4
I first encountered this research a decade ago, but when I revisited it recently, I realized something remarkable: this appears to be a rare case where sociologists and psychologists have discovered the same phenomenon by approaching it from different directions. It’s like we started excavating on opposite sides of the Earth, and now we’ve finally clanged shovels.
On the psychology side, we called this discovery the illusion of explanatory depth. As I’ve written before, people seem to understand the world exactly as well as they need to, and no better. Everyone knows how to use a toilet, for example, but they mistakenly think they also know how a toilet works.
I think this illusion is inevitable, given the architecture of the mind. According to predictive processing theory, the mind is always trying to guess what’s going to happen next, and it only updates its guesses when its expectations don’t match its experience. If you run that algorithm for a while, you’ll end up with a model of the world that is good enough, even if it’s not particularly good. You don’t notice the errors in your model until you run smack-dab into them, and every time you correct one, you assume that you’ve gotten them all.
From the sociology side, this same phenomenon can show up as something like moralistic therapeutic deism. People’s folk morality and folk religion, just like their folk physics, their folk biology, etc., are exactly as detailed as they need to be. Don’t hit, don’t steal, take turns, say please and thank you—almost everyone achieves this basic level of moral development, because otherwise you’ll end up friendless, if not incarcerated. Similarly, almost everyone acquires some vague notion of an all-seeing, sky-dwelling God through simple osmosis. (After all, He is kind of everywhere, literally and metaphorically.)
But beyond a handful of high-level principles, most folks remain mushy on the particulars. Smith and Denton didn’t perform the whole illusion of explanatory depth protocol with their participants, but I’m willing to bet that everyone feels like they have a coherent system of ethical and religious beliefs right up until you ask them any specific questions.
Our value systems are flimsy for the same reason our scientific reasoning is flimsy: we don’t fix our mental models until something tells us that they’re broken. So unless your pastor is popping quizzes during the sermon and cold-calling people in the pews, and unless you find yourself thrust into various Trolley Problems on a regular basis, there’s nothing that tells you that you need to firm up your moral and theological convictions. Why spend your days wondering about right and wrong, good and evil, sacred and profane, etc. when you don’t have to? You’re just going to get yourself into trouble, or even worse, into a philosophy PhD program.
This could explain why our sense of right and wrong is so easily overwritten by any half-decent system of rewards and punishments: we just don’t have much written there in the first place.
So how does anyone ever develop a value system that’s more than a few bullet points? I think, in short, that they look at a fish and they go insane.
YOU MUST LOOK AT THIS FISH AND GO INSANE
You can summarize most of H.P. Lovecraft’s short stories as “Guy looks at something so messed up that he goes totally bonkers.” “Dagon” was among Lovecraft’s first: it’s about a guy who gets marooned at sea and encounters a really freaky fish, which upsets him so much that he ultimately throws himself out a window.
This is a useful metaphor, because I think at the center of everyone’s psyche is some version of the Big Horrible Fish: some unexamined assumption that, if you fully considered it, would require you to upend a significant portion of your life.
I saw my fish in 2020 in San Fransisco, during the annual meeting of the Society for Personality and Social Psychology.5 Inside the conference hotel were dozens of talks about stereotyping, prejudice, inequality, and so on. That had never struck me as strange until that year, when outside of the hotel, which was in the middle of SF’s Tenderloin district, people were sprawled out on the sidewalk, dying of overdoses. Scholars were scurrying past homeless people to give talks on social justice, which is ironic because “scholars will scurry past homeless people to give talks on social justice” is literally the main finding from one of the most famous psychology studies of all time.6
Something un-clicked for me that day. I had assumed that the answer to every dilemma was “more research”, and that eventually, all of the experiments being presented inside the hotel would solve the problems outside of it. But as I ate canapés in a ballroom mere feet from so much misery, I started to wonder whether any of us were even trying to make progress, or whether we were just publishing papers. I still believe that the barrier between us and a better world is a lack of knowledge; I’m just no longer convinced it’s that knowledge. I don’t think we will cure the human suffering visible on the streets of San Francisco by running another thousand studies on stereotype threat, ego depletion, and growth mindset, no matter what wonders it does for our CVs.
I saw many more fish after that, of species varied and grotesque. That’s why, on the rare occasions that I enter the conference hotel these days, my name badge does not have an academic affiliation on it, but instead simply says “guest”.
When I meet someone of uncommon integrity, someone willing to defy the incentives at any cost, I find they almost always have seen the fish—big, hulking fish, far larger than any I’ve ever encountered. They have undergone some kind of moral reckoning that undid their illusion of philosophical depth and gave them the chance to forge their own values. They’re the kind of person who could go to the gallows with a witticism on their lips, the opposite of a loser.
500 DAYS OF SUMNER
I used to see a guy like that every day, although he died a long time ago. Near the psychology department, there was a statue of Senator Charles Sumner, who is most famous for being beaten nearly to death by a congressman from the South in 1856. But that bit of historical trivia doesn’t do justice to the story of his life.
Sumner grows up poor in Boston, living amongst the city’s considerable Black population. On a trip to France in the 1830s, he’s astounded to see Black and white students studying together as equals at the University of the Sorbonne. He writes in his diary: “It must be then that the distance between free blacks and whites among us is derived from education, and does not exist in the nature of things.” He later becomes the most outspoken white abolitionist of his generation, taking positions even his friends think are crazy: the complete and immediate freeing of all enslaved people, followed by Black suffrage7 and racially integrated schools.
Then comes the infamous part: a few days after one of Sumner’s most inflammatory speeches, a congressman named Preston Brooks approaches Sumner at his desk on the Senate floor, accuses him of libel, and then to beats him with a cane until it breaks. Sumner, caught by surprise, is tangled up in his desk and cannot escape; he nearly dies. But then he recovers, and when he does, he becomes even more provocative. In 1861, he pushes Lincoln to abolish slavery in the Confederacy, which causes the newspapers in Sumner’s home state of Massachusetts to call him “a candidate for the insane asylum”. (Two years later, Lincoln issues the Emancipation Proclamation.) Sumner writes bills, arguments, and amendments that are often defeated or defanged, only for them to reappear 100 years later in Brown v. Board of Education and the Civil Rights Act of 1964.8
All that to say: I am guessing somewhere on Beacon Hill, at the Sorbonne, and in the puddle of his own blood on the Senate floor, Sumner saw the fish, and he refused to look away.
PAWS AND CONSIDER
I understand why so many people are so concerned with incentives. It’s infuriating to watch villains succeed. And look, if we can stop rewarding people for doing the wrong things, we obviously should.
But I don’t know if we can. Goodhart’s Law, Campbell’s Law, and their corollaries state that every incentive is destined to be corrupted eventually, and so far, no one has proven these conjectures wrong. That’s why discussions around incentives often sound to me like we’re talking about a monkey’s paw that will grant our wishes, but only in evil, ironic ways. “The last time we made a wish on the Monkey’s Paw, it backfired horrifically. To rectify this, we have decided to make another wish on the Monkey’s Paw.”
In the eternal game of cat and mouse between the goodhearted people trying to fix the incentives and the Goodhart’d people trying to exploit the incentives, I am rooting for the cats. We should check whether our incentive systems are having their intended effects, and we should revisit and revise them accordingly. But for some reason, the second we start talking in terms of incentives, we also start acting like courage doesn’t exist and can’t exist. Bad incentives have become our generation’s version of “I was just following orders”, an excuse that should be an indictment.
So we should try to get our incentives right, but also—incentives be damned, do the right thing. If we seek an end to our permanent problems, we must cultivate in ourselves the same three things Charles Sumner said we should look for in a leader: “The first is backbone, the second is backbone and the third is backbone.”
Shout out to this post from Tal Yarkoni and this tweet from Alice Maz, which I saw long ago and no doubt spiritually inspired this post:
Only morons and cowards “respond to incentives.” Healthy people do what they want to do if reasonably practical, great people do what they want to do no matter what.
It was understood that these helmets, with their gnawed and rotted foam, would offer little protection if you actually got beamed in the head with a baseball. Their role was more ceremonial than functional, like a chef’s toque or a pope’s mitre.
As one participant in Smith and Denton’s study, a Muslim boy from California, put it:
God is like an entity that decides when, if, he wants to intervene with a lot of things. To me God is pretty much like intervention, like extreme luck. Say you’re $50 away from something and you find $50 on the floor, then that’s probably God’s intervention or something like that. But other than that it just seems like he’s monitoring. He just kind of stays back and watches, like he’s watching a play, like he’s a producer. He makes the play all possible and then he watches it, and if there’s something he doesn’t like, he changes it.
Survey research reaches a similar conclusion. For example, Catholics and Protestants spent several centuries murdering each other over doctrinal disputes. Today, however, only about half of Catholics know that they, unlike the Protestants, are supposed to believe in transubstantiation—that the bread and wine used in mass become the literal body and blood of Jesus. Meanwhile, about half of Protestants don’t know who Martin Luther was.
It took place in February, just before covid really kicked off in the US. I remember my advisor cautioning me not to go, and I dismissed him, citing the standard armamentarium of psychological biases: focusing illusion, scope neglect, availability heuristic. When I delivered my apology to him, it had to be over Zoom.
In the 1970s, a pair of psychologists recruited a bunch of seminary students to give a short lecture, either about career opportunities for seminary graduates, or about the story of the Good Samaritan. Some of them were told that they were late to give their lecture and they should hurry, or they were told they were on time or early. On their way to the building where they were supposed to deliver their talk, all the participants passed by a man slumped over in a doorway, groaning and coughing in the December cold. The participants in the “hurry” condition were less likely to stop and help; the content of their talk did not matter. As is common for studies from this era, there aren’t enough participants to be certain these results are robust, but I’m optimistic you could find an effect like this again.
For men, anyway. Sadly, Sumner was never much of an advocate for women. His biographer suggests he was probably gay, and he may have had some resentments toward the opposite sex. He exchanged saucy letters with a male friend of his, and was despondent when that friend married. Sumner himself remained a bachelor until in his 50s, only to have his wife immediately start cheating on him openly and then dump him a few months later. She told everybody he was impotent, which gave his political enemies no end of ammunition.

The pursuit of external incentives often undermines personal integrity, suggesting that individuals should instead cultivate a strong, independent sense of purpose to guide their moral and ethical decisions.

### Key Points
- The author argues that relying on reward systems—or "incentives"—leads to a lack of genuine conviction and encourages people to prioritize status over moral development.
- Research by sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton highlights "moralistic therapeutic deism," where individuals hold vague, unexamined beliefs rather than a coherent value system.
- The "illusion of explanatory depth" suggests that people often overestimate their understanding of complex moral or scientific concepts until they are forced to confront them.
- Senator Charles Sumner is presented as a historical example of someone who defied social incentives to advocate for abolition and civil rights despite facing severe physical violence.
- The author suggests that true moral clarity requires a "reckoning" with uncomfortable truths, metaphorically described as looking at a "Big Horrible Fish."

### Why it Matters
Relying solely on external incentives creates a fragile society where individuals lack the internal backbone to resist corruption or pursue meaningful change. By prioritizing personal conviction over arbitrary reward structures, people can move beyond superficial compliance to achieve lasting, principled progress.

HP redesigned the OmniBook Ultra (again)
And it's mostly good news
HP's top tier has always been a champion of laptop design, and the OmniBook Ultra is no exception. This year it's thinner than a MacBook Air and has edges that taper into (almost) nothingness on most of the sides, except where the ports are. The sides are also diamond-ground flat, so if you love seeing shiny, flat frames around your smartphone, this is the laptop for you.
For such a thin laptop, it has zero chassis flex, which is pretty impressive. It's also cool to the touch no matter how hard the Intel Core Ultra X9 388H works. The haptic touchpad is responsive, and I love that it doesn't dip like the lesser type of touchpad.
There are a couple of issues though. Three Thunderbolt 4/USB4 ports sound good until you realize you don't get USB-A anymore and will need an adapter or a USB-C hub.

Panther Lake does it again, even with a constrained power envelope
This isn't the fastest, but it's still technically impressive

results.title: ★ Retraction: The App Store Rejection of the Week That Was, in Fact, a Correct Rejection
results.author: John Gruber
results.content:
By John Gruber
Yesterday I published an article titled “App Store Rejection of the Week: Dark Hours”. I have retracted it. Its premise was so fundamentally wrong that there’s no point merely correcting or editing it. Even the title, as I explain below, was inaccurate. Although the original is now retracted, I’m not memory-holing it. The text of the original story is available, for transparency and accountability, in plain text (Markdown, natch) and PDF (preserving original presentation). Both of those versions include a preface at the top linking to this retraction. The URL for the original story now redirects to this one that you are currently reading.
To the best of my recollection, this is the first post I’ve retracted in the 24 years I’ve been writing Daring Fireball. I hope it’s the last. I was misled, both overtly and through omissions, in several ways, but what I publish is my responsibility, and I apologize for the error.
Terry Godier first came to my attention in February, when I linked to his excellent interactive essay on RSS feed reader design, “Phantom Obligation”, which essay introduced Current, Godier’s new RSS reader that he made to exemplify the ideas from his essay. Current is, deservedly, a bit of a breakout hit. (E.g., David Pierce, at The Verge, put it on a very short list of iOS-exclusive indie apps that keep him from switching to Android.) In March I linked to another interactive essay from Godier, “The Last Quiet Thing”, and again in April to a post regarding the App Store’s 5-star review system. I struck up an iMessage correspondence with Godier around when I first linked to his work.
Yesterday Godier posted “Browsers Have Standards, the App Store Has Judgment”. As originally published, that post contained these two paragraphs:
  A while ago I tried to submit an iOS app for Dark Hours, my astronomy website for normal people. It was rejected on the grounds that it was astrology.
It has no tarot function, no horoscopes, and nothing that I, or anyone else I’ve asked, would associate with astrology.
Those paragraphs, at this writing (August 8, 11:00 pm ET), have been deleted and replaced by this:
  Note: the original version of this post had a section here about an astronomy app I am working on that began as an astrology app and was rejected after having the astrology content removed. App store [sic] review reached out to me and let me know that they had apparently never been given the updated build and that the app should be fine to submit now.
You can now see the problem that has led me to fully retract my original post, given that my post was entirely predicated on the premise that Godier’s original description of the rejected app was true — that the app “has no tarot function, no horoscopes, and nothing that I, or anyone else I’ve asked, would associate with astrology.” The truth is, the app, as originally submitted by Godier to the App Store (under the name “Asterly”, not “Dark Hours”), was entirely dedicated to astrology, not astronomy, and did in fact include a “Tarot card of the day” feature amongst other occultist horseshit.
The grounds of Apple’s original App Store rejection of the app, and the rejection’s upholding by the App Review Board, were correct.1 I wrongly took Godier at his word, both in his public blog post and in private iMessage correspondence yesterday, that the rejection wasn’t just merely debatable, but completely and rather preposterously ungrounded. Whether Godier ever submitted a build of “Asterly” to the App Store that contained no occult horseshit and only the hard-science astronomy features that were present in his “Dark Hours” website that was available for the last week, I don’t know. But I have no reason to believe that he did.
My disdain for astrology is so utter, and my esteem for Godier’s previous work so high, that it simply never occurred to me that he might have actually made and submitted to the App Store an astrology app, let alone that he’d then feign surprise and frustration that an astrology app was rejected for being an astrology app. I showed him a draft of my post before publication, to make sure I had the story straight, and he offered not a word of caution, only gratitude for my drawing attention to the matter.
It gets messier. Godier’s astrology app that he submitted to the App Store back in January was named “Asterly”. That was still the name when the App Review Board upheld its rejection in April. According to Godier, frustrated by the App Store’s rejection, he ported the astronomy version to the web, launching it last week under the name “Dark Hours” at the domain darkhours.io. (This is why it was incorrect for me, in the very title of my post, to claim that Apple had rejected an app named “Dark Hours”. They rejected an app named “Asterly” and had never seen an app from Godier named “Dark Hours”.) Yesterday, after I linked to Godier’s post and Hacker News then linked to my post, Godier’s “Dark Hours” (with a space) came to the attention (and justifiable surprise) of Miguel Beher, creator of an open-source “astrophotography and dark-sky planner” project named DarkHours (no space). Beher’s GitHub project contains the source code, and the actual web app is freely available at the domain darkhours.app. In an uncomfortable exchange between Beher and Godier on Bluesky, Beher pointed out that Godier’s Dark Hours had the same bug as Beher’s that routed people to “random fields in Mexico”. Earlier today, Godier took his web app down and redirected his darkhours.io domain to Beher’s darkhours.app.
At the end of my now-retracted post yesterday, assuming I had righteously and rightly skewered Apple for an egregiously erroneous App Store review rejection, I wrote:
  Mistakes happen. But in a functioning system mistakes get corrected, and mistakes as obvious as this one get corrected almost instantly and include a quick apology for the conflation.
Obviously it was I who was mistaken. This article is my correction, and I apologize to all who read and believed my now-retracted post, and to the reviewers at the App Store whose competence (if not literacy) I besmirched. I am deeply sorry about that. Won’t happen again.
Regardless of one’s opinion regarding pseudoscience and occultist horseshit — pro, con, or indifferent — one might reasonably think it wrong for Apple to disallow or discourage such apps from the App Store. In fact, there exist plenty of such apps in the App Store, and Apple has even run “Best Astrology Apps” editorial features. Apple’s stance is basically that the App Store has enough of these apps (and I suspect they’re a common source of scams, given that by their very nature they target the gullible). Guideline 4.3(b) states (emphasis added):
  Certain kinds of apps, such as dating, flashlight, sound effects, wallpaper, simple timers, and fortune telling, are well established on the App Store and we will not accept new submissions unless they offer a meaningfully different or improved experience. We may remove these apps from the App Store going forward if they are not updated, improved, or do not attract customers. Other kinds of apps, such as drinking games, Kama Sutra, fart, and burp apps, are mediocre, low-quality, or low-effort and do not add value to the App Store.
That serial comma, ever useful, gives hope to anyone hard at work on a “fart and burp” app. ↩︎

Daring Fireball author John Gruber has retracted a recent article after discovering he was misled regarding an Apple App Store rejection involving developer Terry Godier.

### Key Points
- John Gruber retracted his post about an app named "Dark Hours" after learning the developer, Terry Godier, misrepresented the app's original content.
- The app in question was actually submitted to Apple under the name "Asterly" and contained astrology and tarot features, not astronomy.
- Apple’s App Review Board correctly rejected the submission based on its actual content, contradicting the developer's claims of an unfair rejection.
- Godier also faced criticism for naming his web project "Dark Hours," which infringed on an existing open-source project created by Miguel Beher.
- Gruber apologized to his readers and Apple’s review team for publishing inaccurate information based on the developer's false account.

This incident highlights the risks of relying on unverified developer claims when critiquing platform moderation policies. It serves as a reminder of the importance of due diligence in tech journalism to maintain credibility and avoid spreading misinformation about corporate review processes.

results.title: How Does Formula 1 Qualifying Work?
results.author: Jarrod Partridge
results.content:
Formula 1 qualifying is a three-segment knockout, Q1, Q2 and Q3, that whittles a 22-car grid down to a ten-car shootout for pole position. Each segment eliminates the slowest cars on the clock, and whoever sets the fastest time in Q3 starts the race from the front of the grid. The whole process runs to a single Saturday hour and a half on a standard race weekend, condensing a car’s entire pace advantage or deficit into a handful of timed laps.
- Qualifying runs across three segments, Q1, Q2 and Q3, each shorter than the last, with the slowest cars eliminated at the end of Q1 and Q2 and the fastest ten fighting for pole in Q3.
- The 2026 grid’s expansion to eleven teams and 22 cars changed the cut lines: six cars are eliminated at the end of both Q1 and Q2, rather than the five-and-five cuts of a 20-car grid, though Q3 still seats exactly ten drivers either way.
- Qualifying sets the starting grid, but grid penalties applied afterward can reorder it significantly, and the tyre rule that once forced Q3’s top ten to start the race on their Q2 compound was scrapped back in 2022.
The three-stage format has stayed the same shape since 2006, but the numbers inside it moved with the grid. Q1 runs 18 minutes with all 22 cars on track, and the six slowest are eliminated, filling grid positions 17th through 22nd on the times they set. Q2 runs 15 minutes with the remaining 16 cars, and another six are cut, filling positions 11th through 16th. Q3 runs 12 minutes with the ten cars left, and it is a clean shootout for pole, the same ten-car finale the format has run since it was introduced, just reached by a longer road than it used to be. Whoever sets the fastest time in Q3 starts first: everyone else lines up behind them in order of their Q3 times, or their Q2 times if they didn’t make the cut, or their Q1 times if they went out earliest.
The FIA’s reasoning for moving from five-and-five cuts to six-and-six was straightforward once Cadillac’s entry took the grid from 20 cars to 22: keeping the old cut lines would have either swollen Q3 beyond ten cars or left Q2 with an awkward, uneven field. Six-and-six restores exactly the same ten-car Q3 the format has always used, at the cost of a slightly wider Q1 and Q2 field working through the same 18 and 15 minute windows, which is part of why traffic management has become a bigger talking point among drivers and teams since the change.
The knockout structure itself is not new. F1 tried a single-lap qualifying format from 2003 to 2005, one timed lap each with no second attempt, before a brief and unpopular aggregate format split across Saturday and Sunday sessions lasted just six races later that same year. The three-part knockout arrived in 2006 and has run every season since, though even its session lengths have shifted across the format’s lifetime. What has stayed constant throughout is the underlying principle: fewer cars, less time, higher stakes, right through to a Q3 shootout that has kept the same ten-car shape regardless of how the grid around it has grown or the sessions leading into it have been tuned.
The margins at the very top are tighter than the format’s reputation for late-session drama might suggest. F1 Chronicle’s own analysis of official timing data across the 2026 season shows an average pole margin of just 0.172 seconds across the first eleven qualifying sessions of the year. The tightest of those came at the Hungarian Grand Prix, where Lando Norris took pole by 0.012 seconds, a result that also ended a run of ten consecutive Mercedes poles to open the season, six of them Kimi Antonelli’s and four George Russell’s. The widest margin so far in 2026 sits at the other extreme, 0.317 seconds at the Belgian Grand Prix, a reminder that Q3 shootouts can also settle into something closer to a formality when one car simply has the pace. Both extremes come from the same format applied to the same eleven-team field, which is part of what makes qualifying such a reliable source of genuine, unscripted drama from one weekend to the next rather than a predictable formality on its own.
Q1 is the widest field of the day and the one with the least room for a mistake. All 22 cars are on track together at once, traffic is at its worst because every driver is hunting for the same clear stretch of track at the same time, and a red flag or a blocked lap late in the session can end a season-long campaign for a strong grid slot before it really begins. Drivers typically run a scrubbed banker lap early, a time on the board that guarantees safe passage if conditions worsen, before pushing harder once the track rubbers in and grip improves through the session. Fuel loads stay low and consistent across every run in Q1, since none of it carries any race-strategy implication the way tyre choice further into qualifying does, which keeps the segment a fairly pure test of a single lap rather than a strategic puzzle. The cut here is unforgiving in a way single lap-time comparisons don’t always convey: at the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix, F1 Chronicle’s own analysis of that session’s timing data shows just 0.007 seconds separated the last car to scrape into Q2 from the first car eliminated, with Austria (0.021 seconds) and Britain (0.042 seconds) running almost as close behind it. Those are the moments the elimination format exists to produce.
Q2 plays out with the same knockout pressure on a smaller, generally faster field, since the 16 cars remaining are usually the more competitive runners on the grid that weekend. Traffic eases slightly with fewer cars on track, but the margins for error tighten again because every driver left is capable of a genuinely quick lap, and strategy becomes a bigger factor here than it was in Q1: teams weigh up whether to bank a Q2 time early on a given compound or hold their strongest tyres in reserve for one final push before the chequered flag, and midfield teams in particular often gamble on an earlier lap to avoid getting caught out by a late red flag.
Q3 is the shootout itself, ten cars with nothing left to lose and the shortest window of the day to use it. Most drivers get two genuine attempts at a flying lap, sometimes fewer if traffic or a red flag intervenes, and the whole session tends to compress into a handful of minutes at the end once everyone commits to their final run together. Pole position carries real value beyond the honour of it: translating a front-row start into an actual race win is common, though far from guaranteed, which is exactly why every tenth of a second in Q3 gets fought over as hard as it does.
The grid is built directly from qualifying times, fastest to slowest, but the version published before the race is often not the same order the clock produced. Grid penalties are applied afterward in a defined sequence rather than randomly: driving penalties, such as for impeding another driver during someone else’s flying lap or an unsafe release from the pits, are applied before power unit or gearbox penalties, such as fitting an engine component beyond the number allowed for the season. A driver who picks up a place-drop penalty simply moves back that many places, with everyone between their original and new position moving up to fill the gap, so a single penalty rarely affects only the driver who earned it. Pit-lane starters, drivers required to start from the pit lane rather than the grid itself, are removed from the order entirely and placed behind every other penalised car. A driver who accumulates more than 15 places worth of power unit penalties across a season is sent to the back of the grid outright rather than having each individual penalty applied in sequence.
The grid can also change for reasons that have nothing to do with on-track driving. Cars that finish qualifying near the front go through compulsory post-session scrutineering, covering ride height, plank wear, wing flexibility, weight and fuel samples, alongside a data audit of telemetry against homologated specifications. A breach found during that process can mean disqualification from the session itself, a grid penalty, or a fine, depending on severity, and it is applied on top of whatever the timing screens showed. It is a genuinely different category of consequence from a driving penalty, since a technical disqualification can strip a result that looked entirely clean on track, and it is exactly why teams treat post-session scrutineering as seriously as the lap times themselves. Because that scrutineering and any steward investigations continue after the chequered flag falls on qualifying, the official starting grid is sometimes not confirmed until Saturday evening or even Sunday morning.
Teams work from a fixed allocation of 13 sets of dry tyres across a standard race weekend, covering both practice and qualifying before the race itself draws on whatever is left, and there is no mandated compound for any qualifying segment. Drivers can run whichever dry compound they choose through Q1 and Q2, mixing softs, mediums and hards as their strategy dictates rather than following any prescribed order, and any driver who reaches Q3 receives one additional set of soft tyres specifically for that session. What no longer applies is the rule that used to tie qualifying tyre choice to the race itself: until 2022, the ten drivers who reached Q3 were required to start the race on whichever compound they used to set their fastest Q2 time, a rule that rewarded cars fast enough to scrape into Q3 on a harder, more durable tyre. It was scrapped for the 2022 season after a majority vote among teams, and every driver on the grid has had a free tyre choice for the race start ever since. Wet-weather tyres sit outside that 13-set dry allocation entirely, so a rain-affected qualifying session doesn’t eat into a team’s dry-tyre count for the race, and the extra soft set reserved for Q3 is often the freshest, least-used tyre a driver has access to all weekend, which is part of why Q3 times are typically the fastest of the day even before accounting for a lighter fuel load and a more rubbered-in track.
Sprint weekends add a second, shorter qualifying session, run on Friday rather than Saturday, that sets the grid for Saturday’s sprint race rather than the Grand Prix itself. Sunday’s main race still gets its own separate qualifying session in the usual Q1/Q2/Q3 format, run afterward, entirely independent of how the sprint went. Six rounds carry the sprint format on the 2026 calendar, Miami, Shanghai, Montreal, Silverstone, Zandvoort and Singapore, and the sprint weekend’s full session-by-session format runs to its own set of rules worth reading in full rather than summarised twice.
Any driver who fails to set a Q1 time within 107 percent of the fastest Q1 lap is not automatically entitled to start the race. Race stewards can grant an exception, most often when practice pace or unusual conditions justify it, but the default outcome without one is exclusion from the grid. The rule has not run continuously: it was abolished in 2003, when qualifying moved to a single-lap format that made it largely redundant, and reinstated in 2011 once the current knockout structure made a clear pace baseline meaningful again. In practice it affects the grid rarely, since most cars in 2026’s tighter midfield comfortably clear the threshold, but it remains active regulation rather than a retired one, as Aston Martin found early in the 2026 season when Lance Stroll was initially excluded from the Australian Grand Prix grid before stewards intervened.
Once a car leaves the garage for its first qualifying run, it comes under parc fermé conditions, and those conditions hold until the race itself gets underway. Teams can still make minor adjustments within that window, front wing angle, brake balance and tyre pressures among them, along with repairs to accident or contact damage, and a breach can bring a pit-lane start or a grid penalty of its own. The restricted list runs deeper than the allowed one: parc fermé locks a car’s fundamental setup between qualifying and the race, which is why a car qualifies in very close to the same specification it races in. The clearest exception comes on a weekend where the weather shifts unpredictably between qualifying and the race, one of the few circumstances in which the FIA will relax parc fermé conditions specifically for safety reasons, alongside genuine safety concerns the FIA identifies on its own initiative.

Formula 1’s three-stage knockout qualifying format determines the starting grid for Grand Prix races by eliminating the slowest cars across three segments to crown a pole position winner.

### Key Points
- The format consists of Q1 (18 minutes), Q2 (15 minutes), and Q3 (12 minutes), with six cars eliminated in both Q1 and Q2.
- The 2026 grid expansion to 22 cars necessitated the six-and-six elimination structure to maintain a ten-car shootout in Q3.
- Pole position is awarded to the driver who sets the fastest lap time during the final Q3 session.
- Grid positions are subject to change following post-session scrutineering and the application of various driving or technical penalties.
- Drivers must remain within 107 percent of the fastest Q1 time to qualify for the race, unless granted a specific exception by stewards.
- Parc fermé regulations restrict significant car setup changes from the start of qualifying until the race begins.

### Why it Matters
This knockout system creates high-stakes drama by condensing performance into short, intense windows where even thousandths of a second can dictate a driver's weekend. Understanding these rules is essential for fans, as grid penalties and technical audits often reshape the final starting order long after the checkered flag falls.

results.title: Trump has squandered Republicans’ typical advantages in 2 key areas
results.author: Analysis by Aaron Blake, CNN
results.content:
President Donald Trump’s political stature is so poor right now that he has squandered the Republican Party’s advantage on two major issues that almost always favor the GOP: the economy and national security.
A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week showed Democrats and Republicans virtually tied on “war, foreign conflicts and terrorism.” The GOP led on that issue by 11 points after the 2024 election. Today, 37% of US adults say Democrats have a better approach, compared to 36% who say the GOP does.
Fox News polling a couple weeks back showed something very similar: On national security, 50% of registered voters preferred the GOP, to 48% who preferred the Democratic Party. That’s compared to a 12-point edge for Republicans in January, before the Iran war.
Both recent findings are within the margin of error. But the numbers even being that close is basically unheard of.
Fox polling has regularly tested how registered voters compare the two parties on terrorism and national security. Until the Iran war, Democrats had never even been within double-digits of the Republican Party on either issue.
Republicans have also led consistently on national security in Gallup polling. Democrats only nosed ahead on that issue once in the 21st century: in 2007.
Gallup’s data on which party is better on “international terrorism and military threats” has been even more lopsided in the GOP’s favor.
Across 22 polls conducted since a year after 9/11, Democrats have led on that issue only once — again, in 2007 — and most of the time Republicans led by double-digits.
And then there’s the economy.
The most recent Fox survey showed Democrats leading on that issue by nine points, 54%-45%. That was the biggest Democratic advantage since 2006, when they led by 20 points.
And when they took a lead on the economy back in April, it marked the first time they were ahead since 2010, shortly after the 2008 financial crisis that began during the George W. Bush administration.
CNN polling back in May showed a closer split between the two parties on the economy, with 35% of adults preferring Democrats, compared to 33% who preferred the GOP.
The poll previously asked people to choose between congressional Republicans and congressional Democrats. The last time Republicans didn’t lead on that question was 2009.
The numbers on both fronts seem to illustrate that Trump greatly miscalculated the fallout from launching the Iran war — as well as other controversial policies like his global tariffs.
By launching the tariffs, he effectively took ownership of whatever became of the economic picture. Then he compounded negative public sentiment by basically shrugging off any responsibility to address Americans’ inflation concerns. Now he’s contending with a still-stagnant economic picture, with the economy shedding 23,000 jobs in July.
Americans don’t love Democrats; in fact, the blue side remains pretty unpopular in polls. So the fact that they’ve apparently taken a lead on the economy really says something.
And the national security numbers might be even more striking — because Democrats hardly ever even compete with Republicans on the topic.
Just as education and health care almost always favor Democrats, national security and defending the homeland are almost always signature GOP issues, and lopsidedly so.
That remained true even when Bush launched wars in the Middle East that gradually became pretty unpopular.
Trump, though, seems to have botched the Iran war so badly that Americans suddenly see Democrats on equal footing with the GOP — in terms of issues on the GOP’s own turf.

results.author: EditorDavid
results.content:
In Georgia the Savannah Police Department "terminated four sworn officers and two civilian employees following an internal investigation into misuse of the department's Flock Safety License Plate Reader system," according to a local news report:
All six cases are also under independent criminal investigation by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation... Investigators found that employees were running searches on personal acquaintances and family members. One officer was found to have given someone from an outside law enforcement agency access to SPD's Flock Safety system, which they weren't authorized to do.   
Elsewhere ABC News reports that a female North Carolina police officer was arrested Wednesday "for allegedly using Flock license plate readers to track her boyfriend's ex-wife, according to police..." The officer is accused of accessing the system for personal use 31 different times, including at least twice when she was off-duty, and listing most of the lookups as motor vehicle infractions. [Police chief Ron] Campurciani "added that the department is looking at 10 other potential misuse cases and said three 'look like they could be problematic.'"
 
And an Ohio news station reports a police officer who recently resigned "while under internal investigation repeatedly used the Flock license plate reader system to search a vehicle registered to someone investigators identified as his likely domestic partner."
 
Meanwhile, 404 Media reported this week that an Iowa county's usage police specifically tells police officers — in all capital letters — not to tell occupants of a vehicle that an automated license plate reader was used for a traffic stop. It also instructs officers to not even mention the use of the ALPR technology in their reports "unless absolutely necessary," according to information they'd obtained from a public records request," suggesting they instead they call the cameras "county resources": It is not just local police in small communities who are creating policies designed to obfuscate Flock usage. Earlier this year, we reported that police in multiple states were being told to be "as vague as permissible" about why they were using Flock because their searches could be obtained using public records requests, and that warning was being shared by the FBI and Department of Justice...
 
In the [Iowa county] public records request, Sheriff Don Phillips said "there is no need" to tell people about the use of Flock... results.title: Calgary’s quantum defence bub signals secure communications in Canada
results.author: Dr. Tim Sandle
results.content:
Canada has taken a significant step toward securing its technological future with the launch of the Quantum Defence Innovation Secure Hub (DISH) in Calgary. Backed by $20.3 million in federal funding over two years, the initiative is designed to accelerate the transition of cutting-edge quantum research into practical defence and security applications, with a particular focus on quantum-secure communications.
The announcement places Calgary at the centre of Canada’s growing quantum ecosystem and highlights a broader global race to develop technologies capable of protecting governments, military organizations, and critical infrastructure from emerging cyber threats.
Why quantum security matters
For decades, modern digital communications have relied on public-key cryptography. These encryption systems protect everything from online banking transactions to government communications. However, the emergence of powerful quantum computers threatens to undermine many of the encryption methods currently in use.
While large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers do not yet exist, cybersecurity experts increasingly warn of a “harvest now, decrypt later” scenario, where adversaries collect encrypted information today in anticipation of future quantum systems capable of breaking that encryption. This concern has driven governments worldwide to invest in post-quantum cryptography and quantum-secure communication technologies. Canada has already begun preparing for the transition. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security published a post-quantum cryptography roadmap, while federal departments are being directed to develop migration plans and adopt quantum-resistant cryptographic standards. Against this backdrop, the creation of the Quantum DISH represents more than a research investment. It is part of a national strategy to ensure Canadian defence and government communications remain secure in the quantum era.
The Quantum Defence Innovation Secure Hub is being established under BOREALIS (Bureau of Research, Engineering and Advanced Leadership in Innovation and Science), a federal defence innovation framework. Calgary’s hub is the third DISH facility launched in Canada, following initiatives focused on maritime technologies and uncrewed systems.
Led by a University of Calgary consortium, the facility will bring together researchers, industry partners, innovators, defence organizations, and government agencies. The objective is to create a secure environment where emerging quantum technologies can be developed, tested, validated, and transitioned into operational capabilities for the Canadian Armed Forces. According to National Defence Minister David McGuinty, quantum technologies will fundamentally reshape defence by transforming navigation, communications, sensing, and computing capabilities.
The focus on quantum-secure communications
Among the hub’s priorities, quantum-secure communications stand out as one of the most strategically important. Military communications networks face a growing range of threats, including cyber espionage, interception, and signal disruption. Existing encryption systems may not provide adequate protection against future quantum-enabled attacks. The Calgary hub will therefore support research into communication systems that remain secure even when adversaries possess advanced quantum computing capabilities.
These efforts are expected to include quantum-resistant cryptographic techniques, secure timing and synchronization technologies, and security validation and testing frameworks. Such technologies could eventually protect military command systems, intelligence networks, critical infrastructure, and potentially civilian communications platforms.
The Calgary initiative is not solely focused on communications. The hub will also explore four major quantum technology areas:
- Quantum sensing
- Quantum communications
- Quantum algorithms
- Hardware assurance
Quantum sensing is particularly interesting from a defence perspective. These systems could enable highly precise navigation without relying on GPS signals, which can be degraded, jammed, or spoofed during military operations. The ability to operate independently of satellite navigation has become increasingly important as geopolitical tensions drive concerns about electronic warfare. Hardware assurance activities will seek to validate and test quantum devices and systems before operational deployment, helping ensure reliability and resilience in challenging environments.
Calgary’s selection reflects years of investment in quantum research and innovation. The University of Calgary has emerged as a leading Canadian centre for quantum science through its Quantum City initiative, developed in partnership with government and industry stakeholders. Quantum City has been building infrastructure, commercial partnerships, talent pipelines, and research capabilities designed to accelerate the adoption of quantum technologies. The new defence hub strengthens this ecosystem by creating a direct pathway between academic research and practical national security applications.
University of Calgary President Ed McCauley described the federal investment as “transformational”, highlighting the institution’s established strengths in quantum computing, sensing, and communications. For Calgary, the initiative also reinforces the city’s growing reputation as a technology centre increasingly recognized for innovation in artificial intelligence, clean technology, digital infrastructure, and now quantum technologies.
Economic and strategic implications
The benefits of the Quantum DISH are likely to extend beyond defence. Historically, technologies developed for military applications have often generated significant civilian benefits. Advances in GPS, the internet, and satellite communications all have defence origins. Quantum technologies may follow a similar path. Secure communication techniques, sensing capabilities, and resilient computing platforms could find applications across finance, healthcare, transportation, energy, and telecommunications. The hub may also help strengthen Canada’s domestic technology sector by providing opportunities for startups, researchers, and established firms to collaborate on commercially valuable intellectual property.
Strategically, the initiative supports Canada’s broader goal of technological sovereignty. As countries increasingly compete for leadership in quantum technologies, developing domestic expertise is becoming an important component of both economic competitiveness and national security.
The launch of the Quantum Defence Innovation Secure Hub represents an acknowledgment that the quantum era is approaching faster than many expected. Although practical quantum computing remains an emerging technology, governments can no longer afford to wait until cryptographic vulnerabilities become reality. Nations that invest early in secure communications, resilient navigation systems, and quantum-enabled defence technologies are positioning themselves to maintain strategic advantages in an increasingly digital and contested world.
